issues.legal_issue: An assistant who helps prepare a false official document may be convicted for abetting its preparation even when the official entrusted with preparing it is the principal offender.
material_facts: A public officer was directed to prepare records of the number and value of trees on allotted lands.
The records substantially understated the number and value of the trees.
An assistant attested the allottees’ thumb impressions and helped the officer prepare the records.
The assistant was not the officer entrusted with preparing those records.
The High Court converted the assistant’s conviction from the substantive offence to abetment, and the Supreme Court upheld that conversion.
issues.conclusion: The assistant could not be convicted as the principal offender for preparing the records, but the conviction for abetting the officer’s preparation of false records was proper.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 167 and 109 of the Penal Code, the officer entrusted as a public servant with preparing a document may be liable for knowingly framing it incorrectly, while a person who assists that officer may be liable for abetting the offence. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.officer_entrusted_with_document_preparat: A public officer was assigned responsibility for preparing the official document.
predicates.assistant_helped_prepare_false_document: An assistant helped the officer prepare a document that substantially misstated the relevant facts.
predicates.assistant_not_entrusted_with_document_pr: The assistant was not the official assigned responsibility for preparing the document.
predicates.assistant_conviction_for_abetting_false_: The assistant may properly be convicted for aiding the officer’s preparation of the false document rather than as its principal preparer.

issues.definition: When an assistant helps an officer prepare a false document but was not assigned to prepare it, the assistant may be convicted for abetting the preparation.

issues.legal_issue: A public servant who knowingly makes materially false official endorsements that are relied upon to grant permission and thereby cause wrongful loss may be convicted for framing an incorrect document.
material_facts: The assistant reported that 469 trees were fit to be felled, although the evidence showed that substantially more trees had been cut and many more remained standing.
The assistant knew that the revenue authority would rely on his figures in deciding whether to grant permission to fell trees.
The assistant had prepared the allottees’ applications and did not protest when far more trees were cut than the number for which permission had been recommended.
The Supreme Court upheld the conviction for the false endorsements.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for knowingly making incorrect endorsements with the intention of causing wrongful loss was proper.
issues.legal_principle: Section 167 of the Penal Code applies where a public servant charged with preparing a document knowingly frames it incorrectly with the requisite intention to cause wrongful loss or wrongful gain. The Court inferred knowledge and intention from the grossly inaccurate figures, their expected use by the decision-maker, the excessive cutting, and the assistant’s conduct. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When a public servant knowingly makes a materially inaccurate official report for reliance by a decision-maker and intends wrongful loss or gain, conviction for framing an incorrect document is proper.

issues.legal_issue: The scope of a criminal trial is governed by the charges framed and the notice they give, rather than being confined to the allegations described in the initial complaint.
material_facts: The initial complaint focused on allegedly false records prepared earlier and did not specifically allege that the later endorsements about trees fit to be cut were false.
The formal charges referred to the false records and other false documents, which included the endorsements on the facts alleged by the prosecution.
The accused had notice from the outset that the endorsements were also part of the case against him.
issues.conclusion: The initial complaint did not prevent conviction based on the endorsements because the charges expressly covered them and gave the accused notice of that allegation.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of the trial is ascertained from the charges framed, not limited by the narrower focus of the investigating officer’s complaint, where the charges give the accused clear notice of the conduct relied on. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When the formal charge includes conduct and gives the accused notice of it, that conduct may support conviction even if the initial complaint omitted it.

issues.legal_issue: Acts by a public servant that amount to knowingly making false official records to secure wrongful gain also constitute misconduct under the corruption law.
material_facts: The assistant made materially false endorsements concerning how many trees could be felled, knowing that the figures would guide the permission decision.
The assistant’s conduct formed part of the transactions by which another person obtained the benefit of cutting trees while the public authority suffered loss.
The Supreme Court held that the same acts constituting the false-document offence also constituted misconduct.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for misconduct under the corruption law was proper on the basis of the same acts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(1)(d), read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, covers the public servant’s misconduct established by these acts; the Court stated that the conduct constituting the false-endorsement offence a fortiori constituted such misconduct. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When a public servant uses official duties to make a false record intended to secure wrongful gain or cause wrongful loss, conviction for corruption misconduct is proper.

issues.legal_issue: A person who knowingly assists systematic and extensive unlawful cutting of trees on public land may be convicted for abetting mischief.
material_facts: A contractor and his workers cut trees not only on allotted lands but also on adjoining government lands without authority.
The cutting on government lands was extensive and systematic rather than isolated.

The assistant had been involved from the preparation of the tree records through the applications and arrangements for cutting, and the Court inferred that he knew of the unlawful cutting and did not intervene.
The Court held that the assistant had aided and abetted the mischief, while noting that the issue was academic to the sentences because the substantive sentences ran concurrently.
issues.conclusion: The Court concluded that the assistant had aided and abetted the mischief; consideration of the conviction was academic to the sentence because the substantive sentences were concurrent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 427 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code applies where a person aids or abets mischief. Knowledge and participation may be inferred from the scale and systematic nature of the unlawful cutting and the person’s involvement and acquiescence. No earlier cases are cited.
